step1.title: Regular Expressions
step1.description: Each token type is defined by a regex pattern. These patterns describe what valid tokens look like in Java.

step2.title: Finite Automaton (NFA)
step2.description: Using Thompson construction, each regex pattern is converted into a Non-deterministic Finite Automaton. States and transitions form a machine that can recognize tokens.

step3.title: Fixed Point (NFA → DFA)
step3.description: Subset construction converts the NFA into a deterministic Finite Automaton. The algorithm iterates until no new states are discovered — this is the fixed point.

step4.title: Scanner
step4.description: The DFA scanner reads your source code character by character, transitioning between states. When an accept state is reached, a token is emitted.

pipeline.title: Compilation Pipeline
pipeline.subtitle: HOW JAVA COMPILES YOUR CODE
pipeline.description: Follow the journey from human-readable source code to machine-executable bytecode. Six phases, each transforming your code into something the JVM can understand.
pipeline.completeDescription: In just six phases, your Java source code is transformed from human-readable text into bytecode that the JVM can execute on any platform. This is the magic behind "write once, run anywhere."

source.title: Source Code
source.subtitle: Human-Readable Instructions
source.explanation1: Everything starts with source code — the instructions you write in a programming language like Java. This is text that humans can read and understand.
source.explanation2: Think of it like a recipe written in English. The computer can't follow it directly — it needs to be translated into a language the machine understands.
source.explanation3: The compiler's job is to take this human-readable text and transform it, step by step, into instructions the JVM can execute.
source.javaConcept: In Java, source code lives in .java files. Each file contains a class definition. The compiler reads this file and begins the transformation pipeline.

lexical.title: Lexical Analysis
lexical.subtitle: Tokenization
lexical.explanation1: The lexer (lexical analyzer) reads your source code character by character and groups them into meaningful units called tokens — like breaking a sentence into individual words.
lexical.explanation2: For example, the word 'public' becomes a KEYWORD token, 'HelloWorld' becomes an IDENTIFIER token, and '"Hello, World!"' becomes a STRING_LITERAL token.
lexical.explanation3: This is like how you learned to read: first you recognize individual words before you can understand sentences. The lexer ignores whitespace and comments — they don't affect the program's meaning.
lexical.javaConcept: Java has 67 keywords (like class, public, static, void), identifiers (names you create), literals (fixed values), operators (+, -, =), and separators ({, }, ;). The lexer categorizes every piece of your code.

syntax.title: Syntax Analysis
syntax.subtitle: Abstract Syntax Tree (AST)
syntax.explanation1: The parser takes the flat list of tokens and organizes them into a tree structure called an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST). This reveals the grammatical structure of your code.
syntax.explanation2: Think of it like diagramming a sentence in English class — identifying the subject, verb, object, and their relationships. The AST shows which parts of your code contain other parts.
syntax.explanation3: The tree structure makes it easy for later phases to understand the hierarchy: a class contains methods, methods contain statements, statements contain expressions. Each node knows its type, position, and children.
syntax.javaConcept: Java has strict grammar rules (defined in the Java Language Specification). The parser checks that your tokens follow these rules — for example, that every '{' has a matching '}', and that statements end with ';'. If not, you get a syntax error.

semantic.title: Semantic Analysis
semantic.subtitle: Symbol Table & Type Checking
semantic.explanation1: Semantic analysis checks whether your code actually makes sense — not just grammatically (syntax), but logically. It builds a symbol table: a dictionary of every name in your program and what it means.
semantic.explanation2: Think of it like a glossary for a textbook. When you read 'System.out.println()', the compiler looks up 'System' in its table, finds it's a class in java.lang, then checks that 'out' is a static field of type PrintStream, and that 'println(String)' is a valid method on it.
semantic.explanation3: This phase catches errors like using an undeclared variable, calling a method with wrong argument types, or trying to assign a String to an int. The compiler compares what you wrote against the rules of the language.
semantic.javaConcept: Java is statically typed — every variable must have a declared type, and types must be compatible. The symbol table tracks class names, method signatures, variable types, and scope (what's visible where). This is like a map the compiler builds to understand your program's meaning.

ir.title: Code Generation
ir.subtitle: Three-Address Code (IR)
ir.explanation1: Before generating final bytecode, the compiler creates an Intermediate Representation (IR) called Three-Address Code (TAC). Each instruction has at most three operands: two inputs and one output.
ir.explanation2: Think of it as a simplified, stripped-down version of your code — like reducing a complex math equation step by step. Complex expressions are broken into simple pieces: load this, call that, store the result here.
ir.explanation3: TAC is important because it's a universal format that's easy to optimize. The compiler can rearrange, eliminate redundant operations, or combine instructions at this stage before generating the final bytecode.
ir.javaConcept: In our example, the method call System.out.println('Hello, World!') gets decomposed into: load the System class, access its out field, load the string constant, then call println. Each step is one simple instruction.

bytecode.title: Bytecode
bytecode.subtitle: JVM Instructions
bytecode.explanation1: The final output is Java bytecode — a set of compact binary instructions that the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) can execute. This is what gets saved in .class files.
bytecode.explanation2: Think of bytecode as an assembled recipe — every instruction is precise, numbered, and ready to follow. The JVM reads these instructions one by one and executes them on your machine.
bytecode.explanation3: This is why Java is 'write once, run anywhere' — the same bytecode runs on any device that has a JVM, whether it's Windows, Mac, or Linux. The bytecode is platform-independent; the JVM handles the platform-specific details.
bytecode.javaConcept: The javac compiler produces .class files containing bytecode. You can examine them with javap -c (the Java class file disassembler). Each bytecode instruction is one byte long (hence the name), with opcode 0-255.
